summary: This 1982 memo argues against the claim that international protocol standards already offer a basis for cheap, vendor-supported implementations. It is an opinion piece, originally a MITRE Corporation report, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone says that buying ready-made network software is not as cheap or easy as sellers claim, because the grand promises are bigger than what you actually get.

questions: are vendors supporting international protocol standards
opinion on osi standards versus arpanet protocols
why not wait for iso standards
what are the problems with international protocols
subtitle: Why waiting for vendor-backed ISO standards is a false hope.

tldr.problem: Some argued the DoD should wait for international protocol standards from vendors instead of using ARPANET protocols, expecting cheaper, supported implementations.
tldr.mechanism: M.A. Padlipsky argues this belief is fallacious by showing the ISO/OSI Reference Model suite is incomplete, ambiguous, and less mature than existing ARPANET protocols that have been in real use for years.
tldr.outcome: The opinion paper advocates using proven ARPANET protocols now rather than betting on incomplete international standards, noting vendors have mixed motives for efficiency and clarity.

facts.label: Type
facts.value: Opinion piece, not a protocol specification

facts.label: Main argument
facts.value: ARPANET protocols are proven; ISO standards are incomplete and ambiguous

today: RFC 873 represents the perspective of the early 1980s when TCP/IP and ISO/OSI were competing visions. Despite its skepticism, the ISO/OSI model gained theoretical influence in standards work, while TCP/IP became the dominant protocol suite on the Internet.

sections.title: The Vendor Support Illusion
sections.content:
RFC 873 is an opinion piece from M.A. Padlipsky at MITRE Corporation challenging the view that the DoD should wait for vendor-supported implementations of ISO and NBS international protocol standards instead of deploying the ARPANET Reference Model (ARM) protocols like TCP and IP.

The argument centers on what it means for a protocol to be vendor-supported. The author argues that X.25 alone is insufficient and that a complete protocol suite from NBS or ISO would be needed to compete with the ARMS. The paper then presents four main lines of evidence that vendor-supplied international protocols are not worth waiting for.
sections.plainLanguage: An expert at MITRE argues that waiting for international standards is a bad idea. Companies say they will support these standards, but waiting is a mistake.

sections.title: The Timeliness Problem
sections.content:
The first major problem is timing. The ISO Reference Model Suite (ISORMS) is not complete. Only X.25 (levels 1-3) is firmly established. Proposals for level 4 and above are still in standardization, described as paper protocols never tested in actual use. Even ISO and NBS acknowledge their standards process takes years.

Meanwhile, the DoD operates on long procurement cycles but has an opportunity now. The ARPANET Reference Model protocols exist and have implementations for multiple operating systems already in use. The ARMS can be procured significantly faster than the ISORMS. The author notes that critics who claim the DoD should not develop new protocols are mistaken; the ARMS are not new, they have been in real use for years.
sections.plainLanguage: The ISO standards are not finished yet. Companies must plan purchases years ahead, so waiting means no standards. ARPANET protocols work now, so buying them takes less time.

sections.title: Quality of Vendor Support
sections.content:
Even if waiting were practical, the quality of vendor support for international standards is questionable. The RFC documents specific ambiguities in ISORMS specifications that create interoperability problems: uncertainty about X.25 routing, X.75 gatewaying, expedited data semantics, whether all layers must be traversed on each transmission, whether N-entities must use N-1 entities, and how many protocols exist at each layer.

These ambiguities mean different vendors could implement ISORMS in good faith but have incompatible products. Additional concerns arise from optional features: Vendor A might rely on an optional feature that Vendor B does not supply. In contrast, the ARMS protocols were designed by colleagues who met frequently to resolve ambiguities and refine optional features together. While not flawless, the ARMS are further along than ISORMS.
sections.plainLanguage: The international standards have unclear parts. Different companies could read them differently and make products that do not work together. ARPANET protocols were designed by people who talked to each other, so they fit together better.

sections.title: Design Process and Incentives
sections.content:
The international standards process brings systemic disadvantages. Only active implementers of TCP were allowed on the ARPANET design team, ensuring practical expertise. The international process admits voluntary participation without technical screening, diluting expertise.

The ARPANET protocols also benefited from system programmers working together to conserve resources (CPU, memory) they were trying to make shareable. Vendors, by contrast, have different incentives. The NBS probe mechanism (sending updates every 15 seconds) would have tripled CPU load on early systems. X.25 allows traffic to unrelated nodes. The ISORMS rule requiring N-entities to communicate through N-1 entities multiplies state information unnecessarily. These are not malicious design choices but reflect an environment without positive incentives toward efficiency.
sections.plainLanguage: ARPANET designers were the people actually building systems, so they cared about making them fast and small. Companies care about selling computers and time, so they might make things slower and bigger.

sections.title: The Free Lunch Fallacy
sections.content:
The conclusion is TANSTAAFL: "There Ain't No Such Thing As A Free Lunch." Achieving interoperability between vendor-supplied international protocols will not come for free. Incompatible implementations will need integration work. Maintenance programmers must cope with new operating system releases. The RFC notes that vendors increasingly supply TCP/IP anyway, making the entire question of waiting for international support potentially moot.

Even if international standards eventually become practical, short-term DoD needs are better served by proven ARPANET protocols now.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no free lunch. Everything costs time and money. International standards might be good someday, but using ARPANET protocols now is the practical choice.
